title: Zelensky gives Melania Trump Ukraine's highest award after Oleshky ceasefire
description: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has given the country's highest award for women to the US First Lady, Melania Trump. The Order of Princess Olga
body: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has given the country's highest award for women to the US First Lady, Melania Trump. The Order of Princess Olga, 1st Class, was awarded to Melania Trump for her "significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine", according to the presidential decree. It comes after the end of ceasefire in Ukraine's southern region of Kherson, which allowed for the evacuation of several hundred people from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. Russian and Ukrainian delegations - made up of ombudsmen who were involved in the evacuation mission as well as senior officials - are due to meet at the White House on Thursday on Melania Trump's invitation.The White House said that Melania Trump had "independently initiated engagement between the two warring nations and successfully secured a ceasefire"."This achievement marks an unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American First Lady", it added.Both the Russian and Ukrainian sides repeatedly thanked Melania Trump for brokering the ceasefire, though neither elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement.The delegations travelling to the White House on Thursday will include Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Russian senior official Kirill Dmitriev. Lubinets and Lantratova travelled together into Oleshky last week, in an unusual show of cooperation between Russian and Ukrainian officials. Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament, has previously been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team during peace talks with Russia. He was responsible for informal contact between the White House and Moscow during the ceasefire, according to diplomatic sources quoted by Ukrainian media, and has confirmed he will take part in Thursday's talks.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Russian delegation will be made up of Lantratova and Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian businessman close to the Kremlin who has frequently taken part in US-brokered ceasefire talks. Although both Dmitriev and Arakhamia are veteran participants in high-level peace negotiations, meetings involving such senior representatives are rarely convened through an initiative led by a US First Lady.No details of what the White House event will entail have been shared. "There are important meetings ahead," said Lubinets in a social media post while announcing he was on his way to the US.On Thursday Melania Trump will also deliver remarks on the ceasefire in Oleshky at 11:00 (16:00 GMT), the White House website said.Zelensky's decree also cited Melania Trump's wider humanitarian work, including her efforts concerning Ukrainian children affected by the war, as reasons for giving her the Princess Olga award. Melania Trump has largely remained discreet on foreign policy matters, but in 2025 she said an "open channel of communication" had been established with Russian President Vladimir Putin, allowing for Ukrainian children displaced in the war to be reunited with families.Earlier this year the UN said the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia constitutes a crime against humanity and a war crime. According to Ukraine, almost 20,000 children have been illegally sent to Russia and Belarus since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Russian, Ukrainian and American representatives are also going to meet in Abu Dhabi next week in the first trilateral meeting since February. The talks will be focused on postwar security agreements and de-escalation, US envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.

schema.headline: Zelensky gives Melania Trump Ukraine's highest award after Oleshky ceasefire

title: Rwanda's army team removed from BAL after US sanctions, NBA says
description: The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in
body: The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March. The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.The BBC has asked Rwanda for comment.In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda."What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked. Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports. The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the BAL in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba. It is a professional league featuring 12 club teams from across the continent.Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.

schema.headline: Rwanda's army team removed from BAL after US sanctions, NBA says

title: Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted 'no to war'
description: Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US has said that Americans have "said NO TO WAR", after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a
body: Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US has said that Americans have "said NO TO WAR", after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a stunning defeat in the midterm elections."We endorse this message," parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X."If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," he warned.Trump acknowledged on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in petrol prices. But he insisted that he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran in February.Iran's Supreme Leader said he did not expect US policy to change after the results. Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since the Iran war began, released a statement saying anyone who thinks there will be any change from American "hostility towards the Iranian nation" is "gravely mistaken". In an interview with Fox News, Trump said of the midterm results: "I think a part of it was Iran".He went on to say: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."Speaking separately to the BBC's US news partner, CBS News, Trump said the conflict would end "when I say it ends".In recent weeks, the president has warned that the US and Israel could return to all-out war after the midterms if a deal to end the conflict cannot be reached with Iran.Also on Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.The IRGC said two of the vessels were still burning, and two additional tankers had been intercepted, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. It said they were trying to travel through a prohibited southern route in the Strait of Hormuz.BBC Verify has been investigating the IRGC claims, and has not found any evidence that four tankers were destroyed. In a separate incident, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre said a tanker was struck by two unknown projectiles about 14 nautical miles (26km) north-east of Limah, in Oman's Musandam peninsula, on Tuesday evening. No casualties were reported, it added.On Monday, an Indian crew member of a dhow - a wooden sailing boat - was killed in an attack north-east of Limah. Thirteen other crew members were rescued by Omani authorities.The IRCG also reported on Wednesday that its forces had shot down another US MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz.It made a similar claim on Monday night, when US officials said the US military had carried out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.In an interview with the Financial Times ahead of the midterms, Trump suggested he was happy with the state of the conflict, and that he did not consider them to be "really in a war".When asked about what the newspaper described as "strong hints" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be an attack on Iran this week, Trump said they were "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".Indirect talks to end the conflict have been stalled for months.President Masoud Pezeshkian maintained on Tuesday that his government had been trying to resolve the crisis "through dialogue"."No-one will benefit from this war" if it were to resume, he warned.He also emphasised that Iran's supreme leader had granted the government powers to negotiate "issues that he had previously considered off-limits".Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqai said on Monday that the basis of the current indirect negotiations mediated by Qatar remained a seven-step proposal that Iran submitted in September. But he added that the proposal had been "condensed, making it possible to implement it within two days".The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the Strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Additional reporting by Gabriela Pomeroy

schema.headline: Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted 'no to war'

title: All's Fair: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'
description: "We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is the
body: "We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian bearing the brunt of criticism.The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand.Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down."I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life, after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification."If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice, external, she does say she will change how public she is about her studies."I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton. "I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me. "I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.As for Kardashian's acting, Watts says she's on a "trajectory" that sees her "stepping up in the second season"."She was improvising, riffing, doing all kind of things that I thought were deeply impressive," Watts adds, to which Kardashian jokes: "I think I'm just naturally so funny."One of the positives that critics did cite was the show's desire to spotlight the duality of professional women who were both feminine and successful, which Kardashian says she "loves" because it is "a really realistic depiction of a lot of women I know"."It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

schema.headline: All's Fair: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'

title: Florida Republicans fend off Democrats as state elects first black governor
description: FOLLOW LIVE - Election results and analysis RESULTS - Live US 2026 midterm results as they come in ANALYSIS - Democrats push deep into Republican terr
body: FOLLOW LIVE - Election results and analysis RESULTS - Live US 2026 midterm results as they come in ANALYSIS - Democrats push deep into Republican territory with historic winsNixon had scored a surprise win in the Democratic primary to become her party's standard-bearer, although her campaign funding could not match Moody's, who came out on top.Donalds had served in Congress since 2021 before running for governor to replace long-serving Republican Governor Ron DeSantis, who was term limited and could not run again. A big supporter of Trump, Donalds was at one point on the short list to be his running mate in 2024.Born in Brooklyn, he moved to Florida for university and became a fixture in local politics before running for Congress.Democrats in the state had some surprise wins, too. Republicans in Florida had helped redraw political voting maps as part of a national redistricting push to boost each political party's chances of taking seats in the House. But in all three districts that were redrawn to help Republicans, Democrats held on to their seats.

schema.headline: Florida Republicans fend off Democrats as state elects first black governor

title: James Talarico becomes first Democrat to win Texas Senate seat in decades
description: LIVE: Follow latest updatesRESULTS: The latest from around the countryREACTION: Ecstatic scenes and historic momentsGUIDE: What are the US midterms?In
body: LIVE: Follow latest updatesRESULTS: The latest from around the countryREACTION: Ecstatic scenes and historic momentsGUIDE: What are the US midterms?In a further, historic victory for Democrats in the state, Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott - one of the nation's highest profile governors and a long-standing Trump supporter.At a watch party in Austin, the state's capital, there were jubilant scenes among Talarico supporters as giant television screens projected him the winner on Tuesday night.Supporters hugged, they kissed, and they drank to a reality that many say they dared not believe would come true.Emerging on stage to rapturous applause at his official watch party at a nearby performing arts theatre, Talarico pronounced: "We just took back Texas.""We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas," he continued, referring to his win over Paxton whose campaign was backed by Elon Musk, the world's richest man.He invoked religious themes that have grown familiar to his campaign, comparing his unlikely odds to the biblical story of David and Goliath."This win, this win is for every Texan who's ever wondered if anyone is listening," he said. "I hear you, we hear you. And tonight the world hears you."For decades, the idea of a Democrat winning a statewide race had felt like a pipe dream for Texas liberals. As the nation's second most populous state, Texas has been a bastion of conservatism, routinely rolling out Republican policies that are later employed elsewhere. But throughout the campaign, polls suggested state legislator Talarico was breaking through with voters, energising a Texas Democratic base desperate for new leadership. Spending in the race skyrocketed, and it quickly grew to become the most expensive US Senate race in history, with more than half a billion dollars spent. Billionaire Elon Musk poured in $158m (£117m) to a super PAC supporting Paxton's campaign - a point that Talarico used in attacks on Paxton's campaign. Speaking to CBS on Wednesday morning after his victory, Talarico said Musk "wanted a senator who was going to do his bidding, who was going to sell off Texas land to his data centers, who was going to give [away] our Texas water"."I think last night the people of Texas delivered a crystal clear message to the world's first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale," he said. Then two members of the Bush family, the Republican political dynasty that counts Texas as its political launchpad, backed Talarico in a stunning move foreshadowing Paxton's doom.George Washington University political science professor Quardricos Driskell told the BBC that Paxton was a major part of Republicans' downfall, calling him an "objectively terrible candidate". He said the win in Texas by Talarico, combined with another upset on Tuesday that ousted the state's Republican governor Greg Abbott, was "absolutely historic". Abbott's loss marked the first time a Democrat had won a race for governor in the state since the 1990s. "This wasn't just a tsunami, not just a referendum, but this was a bloodbath," Driskell said about Democrats gains in the Lone Star State. "A clear distinction that the country wants to go in a different direction". Talarico defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary. Then continued to maintain good polling numbers despite an onslaught of negative adverts, including attacks on past comments where he supported transgender people. Throughout his campaign, he frequently leaned into his religious upbringing – as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary – sprinkling his stump speeches with biblical references.Paxton had been beleaguered by a number of political scandals, including his impeachment by his own party in 2023 on corruption accusations, before he was later acquitted by the state's Senate. He was also indicted by the US Securities and Exchange Commission on federal fraud charges, but they were later dismissed.Trump made multiple stops in Texas to beef up support for Paxton and other Republicans - including in reliably-Republican spots, signalling how concerned party leadership was about turnout. Voters have been frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.Hispanic voters and those who live along the southern US border have also taken issue with Trump's immigration policies. Despite border crossings plummeting under Trump - something that had been popular with Texas voters - polls suggested Trump's support among Hispanics, who make up a third of the state's population, had ebbed significantly.Surveys taken since late summer indicated a majority of Texan Hispanic voters - many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 - now disapproved of the president. They also suggested that Hispanic voters were favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin.Many Texas Hispanics who spoke to the BBC before the election pointed to Trump's immigration crackdown as the reasoning behind their change of heart. They pointed to aggressive measures that led to citizens being detained and non-violent offenders being rounded up indiscriminately.Reacting to the result on Truth Social, Trump wrote: "If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn't become a RINO [Republican in name only] in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn't have lost."

schema.headline: James Talarico becomes first Democrat to win Texas Senate seat in decades

title: Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins in Michigan to become first Muslim senator
description: The former public health administrator campaigned on a left-wing platform that included universal health care and a wealth tax on billionaires.The win
body: The former public health administrator campaigned on a left-wing platform that included universal health care and a wealth tax on billionaires.The win comes days after El-Sayed's Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens,  endorsed Rogers, the Republican candidate, just days before the election.El-Sayed's supporters gave deafening cheers when he took to the stage, as they chanted his name in jubilation. A sea of iPhones were held up to take in this moment of history - a Muslim man elected to the Senate.Several people in the crowd embraced, filled with emotion. They repeated his slogan back to him like they were at a concert: "Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all." On the campaign trail, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, described Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide and called for an end to US aid to the country. The issue carries particular resonance in Michigan, which is home to the second largest Arab-American population in the US. It also fuelled tensions between El-Sayed and Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, whose primary campaign received millions of dollars in backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).The contest was widely seen as a test of the political influence of the Democratic left in a key battleground state, following a series of primary wins by democratic socialist candidates in more politically favoured districts.This is a milestone for Muslim Americans who had to watch, along with their children, as El-Sayed was attacked with increasing anti-Muslim rhetoric, including directly from the president of the United States. It comes at a time of rising in Islamophobia nationwide.Roula Allouch, an Arab American Muslim, told the BBC she had goosebumps from the success of the campaign. "I'm proud of Abdul, the campaign that he ran, his family for their perseverance through all the hate, the Islamophobic rhetoric that was thrown at him throughout this campaign," she said. Another Muslim woman in the crowd was equally moved and told the BBC his win meant everything to her. "He makes us so proud and it just makes us feel like we can stand a little taller, broaden our shoulders and know somebody has our back and that he's going to be in Washington really fighting for us," she said. El-Sayed has certainly shown on the campaign trail that he's willing to hit back at Maga attacks. In his victory speech, he used the Arabic phrase "Alhamdullah", and then trolled Republicans by saying that "for the rightwing ops, that just means praise be to God". El-Sayed, 42, represents a generation of Arab Americans and Muslims who were born in the United States to immigrant parents and grew up in post-9/11 America.Celebrating with family from Chicago, another South Asian Muslim supporter of El-Sayed's said the moment was historic for everyone who has been made to feel that they don't belong in America or have a place in politics. "If someone with the name of Abdul can make it, that means this next generation can look up and say that they can too," she told the BBC.The Michigan Senate seat, previously held by retiring Democrat Gary Peters, was considered by analysts to be one of the tightest races in Tuesday's midterm elections. El-Sayed's win further cements Democrats' control of the US Senate after a wave of wins - including in deep-Republican areas. He had to contend with massive outside spending heavily favouring Rogers and his opponent in the Democratic primary, Haley Stevens. He's been unapologetic and unwavering in his stances.In presidential elections, Michigan is one of the crucial swing states - the state voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but Donald Trump in 2024.Many had questioned whether Stevens' last-minute endorsement of Rogers would make a difference in the race.Democratic leadership called it "a despicable betrayal" and her staff reportedly resigned in mass. Voters who spoke with the BBC in the state said they were confused over the move, with some questioning whether the congresswoman was acting out of anger. El-Sayed attempted to ignore the dramatic turn, telling reporters that he doesn't "think about Haley Stevens" and "none of this matters".

schema.headline: Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins in Michigan to become first Muslim senator

title: South Africa local elections: ANC under pressure to reverse decline
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 500 parties are contesting the electionsByKhanyisile NgcoboReporting fromJohannesburgUpdate
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 500 parties are contesting the electionsByKhanyisile NgcoboReporting fromJohannesburgUpdated 4 hours agoSouth Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes. Election officials say voting is going smoothly, despite long queues at some polling stations.Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral."What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.Image source, Khanyisile Ngcobo/BBCImage caption, Sanele Ntombela (left), seen here with his friends Tshiamo Mbange (centre) and Lwandle Dladla, is excited to cast his voteWe found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change."We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The ANC faces immense pressure to reverse years of declineThe BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision."It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity. "Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention". "If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.Melanie VerwoerdThe expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever doneOf South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.But that might change.Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC."And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.Image source, Khanyisile Ngcobo/BBCImage caption, Zandile Mncube says things have got worse in her township over the yearsVerwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros."We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa's elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline.Ndou attributed this to the "calibre" of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns.South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.

schema.headline: South Africa local elections: ANC under pressure to reverse decline

title: Air pollution: Indian capital Delhi's air quality worsens ahead of Diwali festival
description: Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.The city
body: Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, northwesterly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external Twitter, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: Air pollution: Indian capital Delhi's air quality worsens ahead of Diwali festival

title: Javits Frimpong: Mother flies from Ghana to the US to seek justice
description: His mother was escorted to the airport by relatives and Dr Erieka Bennett, Head of Mission of the African Diaspora Forum."I'm going to America to plan
body: His mother was escorted to the airport by relatives and Dr Erieka Bennett, Head of Mission of the African Diaspora Forum."I'm going to America to plan my son's funeral," Gyamfi said.She thanked the government and well-wishers for their support and prayers following her son's death.In a social media post on Saturday, New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said Trump had agreed to grant a visa to Gyamfi so she could mourn her son in person.Mamdani said the murder of a child was a pain no parent should endure, "let alone from thousands of miles away.”"Javits Frimpong's mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump, and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately," he said."All of New York City is mourning this tragedy," he added.Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it was following the case closely to ensure justice.It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators are brought to justice.Police are searching for three teenage suspects who fled the scene, captured on surveillance footage.The shooting has sparked concern among Ghanaians about the safety of children sent to study in America.

schema.headline: Javits Frimpong: Mother flies from Ghana to the US to seek justice

title: Hungary opens secret police files, 47 years after fall of communism
description: Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itsel
body: Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule. Critics say it has come too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members. The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution."I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity,"  Prime Minister Péter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest."Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer. Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided. Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary. Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.Krisztian Ungváry, a historian who has long campaigned for the full release of the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power."In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna Borvendég, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party. Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.

schema.headline: Hungary opens secret police files, 47 years after fall of communism

title: Rafael Nadal: Tennis legend set to join Real Madrid board of directors
description: Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.Nadal won 22 Grand Slam titles, two Olympic gold medals and
body: Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.Nadal won 22 Grand Slam titles, two Olympic gold medals and helped Spain claim five Davis Cups before retiring in 2024.Real's members will be asked to approve the 40-year-old's appointment to the board at a meeting later this month.In a statement announcing the move, external, the club said Nadal was "one of the greatest legends in the history of sport and one of the most admired and recognised Spanish athletes in the world"."It is a great source of pride that a figure of his sporting and human stature, a benchmark of Spanish and world sport, will become part of our board of directors and contribute, from this position of responsibility, to the present and future of our club," Real added.The tennis legend - a boyhood Real fan who holds member's number 67,778 - included a photo of himself as a child in a club kit in his response to the news."I want to thank president Florentino Perez and the board for proposing that I join the board of directors of Real Madrid," Nadal said in his post on X, external."I have accepted this proposal with great excitement, a desire to learn, and a willingness to contribute everything I can."It is currently unclear as to what responsibilities Nadal would hold on the club's board.Perez was re-elected to serve a new four-year term as Real president in June, having held the office since 2009.He swiftly appointed Jose Mourinho to a second spell as head coach, hoping to improve the club's fortunes after they went a second season without a trophy in La Liga, the Champions League or the Copa del Rey.Real are currently third in the league after 11 games - three points behind defending champions Barcelona.

schema.headline: Rafael Nadal: Tennis legend set to join Real Madrid board of directors

title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night
description: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByNorth America correspondentUpdated 8 hours agoDemocrats have torn up Donald Trum
body: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByNorth America correspondentUpdated 8 hours agoDemocrats have torn up Donald Trump's political map on a night that will send shockwaves through American politics for years to come.With a string of major Senate victories in states that have been reliably Republican for decades - and in Kansas's case, nearly a century - a blue tidal wave crashed across the nation, sweeping Republicans out of power.Halfway through President Donald Trump's second term, the Democrats now have decisive control of the House of Representatives and have wrested a majority back in the Senate. They will be able to frustrate Trump's agenda, and launch investigations into his administration. A historic third impeachment attempt could also be on the cards.Few imagined such an outcome was possible in the months after Trump returned to the White House with unified Republican control of Congress in January 2025. As the public mood turned against him and his party, Democrats had hopes of retaking the House.But they contemplated a Senate map that appeared unfriendly, populated by states Trump had won comfortably just two years ago.Instead, Democrats rewrote the political equations with victories in Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina.In comments to the BBC's US partner CBS, Trump pledged to strike deals with congressional Democrats, adding that he didn't want to have to spend his final two years in office rejecting their legislation.He somewhat undermined that sentiment later, posting a picture to Truth Social of his trademark red baseball hat with the word "veto" emblazoned on it.The president went on to note that his name wasn't on the ballot this year, but if it had been Republicans would have won a decisive victory. Trump had helped elevate many of those Republican candidates, however, and had urged voters to pretend he was up for re-election.LIVE: Follow latest updatesREACTION: Trump accepts Democrats did a 'good job' in electionTHE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key resultsGUIDE: What are the US midterms?In the Senate, Democrats flipped at least six seats, comfortably securing a majority.Adam Hamilton won in Kansas - a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate almost 100 years ago during the Great Depression.James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race, ending a 38-year Democratic losing streak in statewide elections there.In South Carolina, Annie Andrews beat Darline Graham, who had been appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham. Few analysts had that seat in play even a few months ago.Five-term Republican Susan Collins conceded Maine's Senate election to Democrat Troy Jackson.Paralympian Josh Turek flipped the Iowa Senate seat held by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Democrats also wrested from Republicans a Senate seat in Ohio, with Sherrod Brown's comeback victory over Jon Husted.Meanwhile, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has beaten Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's bitterly fought Senate race.Nor was that the end of the electoral carnage for Republicans. Ruby-red Texas witnessed another seismic result in the governor's race.Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, who was earlier this year seen as the prohibitive favourite.Democrats also took governors' races in Iowa, Ohio and Georgia, which made history by electing the first black woman to such a post.Meanwhile, the party has won a House majority for the first time since 2022.They are projected to win 245 House seats and the Republicans 166 seats.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democrats celebrate in Maine where the party won a crucial Senate raceA look at the key races offers plenty of reasons why.Democrats flipped House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Kentucky and Colorado, among others. And they were poised to make gains in Virginia and Indiana. Black Democrats in the southern states turned out in record number, helping to carry their party to victory. And Hispanic voters, whose support had helped secure Trump's presidential victory in 2024, swung decisively back to the Democrats.Democrats won all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border. And Hispanic voters helped Democrats hold House seats in Florida that the state's Republicans had sought to flip by redrawing the congressional district lines.In fact, the congressional redistricting battles that had dominated headlines for months last year ended up being a bust for the Republicans. In Texas, they had hoped their line-drawing would net five new seats for their party. But on Tuesday they may end up losing one seat.If there is a silver lining for conservatives, Florida as a whole still appears to tilt to the right.Republican Senator Ashley Moody narrowly won re-election, as did congressman Byron Donalds, who was elected the Sunshine State's first black governor. And embattled Republicans were able to hold governorships in Vermont and New Hampshire. But the bright spots were few and far between.Just two years ago, Trump won the presidency with 48% of the vote. He claimed an electoral mandate. He then went about governing like it, pushing sometimes unpopular policies on trade and immigration, and launching an Iran war that is opposed by most of the American public.On Tuesday, voters gave him the kind of stinging rebuke that will not be easily forgotten.Figure caption, BBC asks voters across US what brought them to the polls todayFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night

title: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
description: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByDaniel BushWashington correspondentInside the Republican Party, initial shock
body: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByDaniel BushWashington correspondentInside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night quickly gave way to anger with US President Donald Trump.After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress."It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told the BBC. "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this."Most Republicans expected to lose control of the House and were clear-eyed about the challenge of holding onto the Senate in a tough election cycle that favoured the party out of power. But some said in interviews that Trump dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington."It was just one mistake after another," said Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota. "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."A White House ally said public disapproval with Trump over the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm" in November."There's palpable frustration [within] the party about how this has all played out," the person said, and much of it is directed at Trump. Anger with Trump "is extremely high".FOLLOW LIVE: Election results and analysis of the US midtermsAnthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland Key moments from a night of midterm election firstsFive reasons why Trump did so badlyThe BBC spoke to a dozen party operatives, campaign officials, White House allies and others, many of whom spoke on background to offer a candid assessment of Trump's approach to the midterms.Trump and Republicans had a lot riding on the outcome on Tuesday night. A stronger showing by the president's party - as happened in 2022, when Democrats under then-President Joe Biden lost just nine seats in the House, and gained one in the Senate - would have given Republicans some momentum heading into 2028.But Trump will instead face a motivated Democratic majority in Congress that is eager to investigate the administration, block his judicial nominees and stymie the rest of his agenda. The midterms have ushered in an uncertain new phase in Trump's second term and may force Republicans to start grappling with their post-Trump future.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The result amounted to a rejection of Trump, one top Republican lobbyist said"I don't think his influence is slipping," said Steve Scheffler, the Republican National Committeeman in Iowa, speaking on the eve of the election. Still, he said, when it came to the midterms, "there were things you wish he said differently".Trump was silent for much of the night before posting a message on Truth Social after the House and Senate were called for Democrats."I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote.He said in later interviews with the New York Times and Fox News that he would accept the election results. Trump told Fox he was a "little bit surprised" by the election results, but noted that the president's party typically fared poorly in midterm elections.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Republican Senator Jon Husted at an election event in Ohio, where the Senate seat flipped in favour of Democrat Sherrod BrownSince 1934, the party in the White House has only gained seats in three midterm elections. While the Democratic gains in 2026 did not set a record, the party did win dozens of House races, state governor contests and Senate seats, including in states where the party had not been competitive for decades.Before Tuesday, Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and had not won a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. The party also notched surprise upsets in other reliably red states like South Carolina that were thought to be safe seats for Republicans just weeks before Election Day.Trump and Vice-President JD Vance held dozens of campaign rallies in the run-up to the midterms. The principal Trump-aligned Super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent hundreds of millions backing Republican candidates.Trump allies said it was unfair to hold him responsible for the party's election losses. They pointed to the history of midterm elections, and said the party was saddled with weak Republican candidates in battleground states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas.Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, ran "the worst Senate campaign in the country from either side of the aisle," said another Texas Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "If Ken's campaign knocked on 100,000 doors I'd be shocked," the source said. The person added that Paxton's victorious Democratic opponent, James Talarico, ran "a really good and smart campaign."Others defended Trump's autumn campaign schedule, noting that he had to balance his day job of running the country with midterm travel."He's the president. He's not going to spend his time campaigning 24/7," said Krish Mathrani, the Michigan Republican Party's youth chair. Mathrani said Trump's campaign rallies helped drive up enthusiasm among Republican voters. "President Trump is a turnout machine," he said.That's true in presidential elections. But Trump's vaunted turnout operation has failed to deliver in elections when he's not on the ballot, and 2026 proved no different.Voters rejected Trump's argument that the economy was better on his watch and that he was achieving his aims in the war with Iran. The effort by Trump to portray Democrats as extreme socialists also fell flat, as voters handed victories to moderates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina."That just didn't work with Cooper," said a Cooper campaign official. "Trying to tag him as some socialist liberal, that wasn't going to fly."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Republican supporters at a watch party in Iowa, where Democrat candidate Josh Turek won a Senate seat Trump often seemed disinterested in the midterms over the summer, the period of time when Republicans in Congress shifted their focus to the election. Trump was consumed by the war with Iran abroad and his construction overhaul of Washington at home. The projects included the under-construction ballroom and a helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, renovations to a local golf course, a proposed memorial arch near Arlington Cemetery and renovations to the Kennedy Center.Events like a UFC match at the White House on Trump's 80th birthday in June created the impression that the president was more interested in feting himself than winning the midterms, several sources said. Trump also repeatedly downplayed the rising costs of gas and often cast the affordability issue as a Democratic hoax.Trump turned his full attention to the election in September at the Republican Party's midterm convention. The event was a gamble: Republicans hadn't held a midterm convention in decades, and it was an open question whether voters would tune in.Trump dominated the convention in Dallas, frustrating Republicans who told the BBC they wanted to highlight the party's midterm candidates. In his rambling keynote speech, Trump pledged to give $5,000 (£3,700) to anyone who voted for Republicans and raised eyebrows with an endorsement of Paxton which included a lengthy criticism of the candidate's lack of charisma and physical appearance."Obviously, that's never helpful," Robin Armstrong, Texas' Republican National Committeeman, said of Trump's critique of Paxton. "You're not going to stop what President Trump says. We just have to kind of live with that."The convention failed to attract a large television audience, and Democrats were quick to call it a failure. "It backfired for Republicans because nobody paid any attention to it," said Terri Burke, the Texas Democratic Party's executive director.Trump's penchant for straying off-message continued when he hit the campaign trail in the final weeks before Election Day. He made headlines for praising Ohio Republican Senator John Husted's physique, and drew criticism for calling Abdul El-Sayed a "jihadist" in the Michigan Senate race.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mike Rogers in Michigan was among the other losing candidates - having been beaten to a Senate seat by Democrat Abdul El-SayedAs Trump criss-crossed the country stumping for Republican candidates, the White House contended with controversies in Washington. Katie Zacharia was ousted after just five days as White House press secretary, and Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the US ambassador to Greece after reports surfaced that she asked a donor to pay her credit card debt.Trump also faced a backlash in October for striking a deal to buy Russian diesel. The agreement, which blindsided members of Congress and drew condemnation from some Republicans, came just weeks after Trump signed a sanctions bill aimed at cutting off Russian oil and gas revenue.Democrats used the deal and other scandals swirling around the White House to make the case for retaking control of Congress. The messaging resonated in the end, as Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress in convincing fashion.A second White House ally said that the president's political aides projected optimism until the final days of the election, even as it became clear the party was headed to defeat.Now, as Republicans take stock of the loss, several said they were ready to look ahead to the 2028 election."Whether that's JD Vance, or Macro Rubio, or Ted Cruz, we've got a pretty big bench," said Scheffler, the state's RNC member. "It'll be a wide open race."Peppin, the Republican strategist, said the midterms results demonstrated the party needed a new direction. "I sincerely hope that we've turned the page from the Trump era, and that we'll have new players, new issues and a new focus moving forward."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton was defeated by Democrat James Talarico in Texas

schema.headline: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat

title: Everything you need to know from the US midterm elections
description: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByJames FitzGerald and Nardine SaadReporting fromLos Angeles, CaliforniaUpdated
body: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByJames FitzGerald and Nardine SaadReporting fromLos Angeles, CaliforniaUpdated 1 hour agoDemocrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.Projected results have provided the party with a number of things to celebrate - and rival Republicans some reasons to commiserate. Here is everything you need to know about some of the big Democratic wins and some historic firsts.Democrats toast victories in deep-red Trump countryImage source, ReutersImage caption, James Talarico, the new US senator in Texas, and Gina Hinojosa, the state's new governor, toast their successesTalarico's supporters went beserk as the projected results arrived at an election-night party, wrote the BBC's Gary O'Donoghue. Attendees hugged, kissed and drank to a reality they dared not believe would come true.Hinojosa became the first Latina to be elected governor of the state.Among the other states where history was made by the Democrats were Kansas, where Adam Hamilton took a closely-fought Senate seat - giving the state its first Democratic senator for nearly a century.LIVE: Follow latest updatesREACTION: Trump accepts Democrats did a 'good job' in electionANALYSIS: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic nightGUIDE: What are the US midterms?Senior party figures who cheered the results included Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the Speaker of the lower chamber of Congress."Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters. If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next Speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Johnson and becoming the first black person to fill that role.Trump congratulates opposition and acknowledges Iran and fuel prices were issuesTrump spoke throughout the evening to a number of US media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job".He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Congress. Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."He acknowledged that the US-Israel war on Iran, which has impacted consumer prices in the US, had affected the vote. Trump argued that high fuel prices meant voters could not see how well his economy was doing "as much as they should have", adding: "The gasoline was caused by Iran."El-Sayed wins US Senate race in Michigan after fellow Democrat turns on himAbdul El-Sayed has become the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate - after claiming victory in Michigan in what was one of a handful of closely fought contests. His win means the seat stays in Democratic hands. He defeated Republican opponent Mike Rogers, who received the surprise backing of El-Sayed's Democratic rival in the primary contest, Haley Stevens, who changed her endorsement at the eleventh hour.The race was one of the bitterest of the midterms. Trump invoked 9/11 and even called El-Sayed a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.Image source, ReutersImage caption, El-Sayed triumphed in one of the bitterest contests of the midtermsEl-Sayed's supporters went wild when he took the stage to celebrate his claimed victory, wrote the BBC's Nada Tawfik. He said: "Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say 'inshallah,' or 'God willing,' whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned." He went on to say: "But today, tonight, we can turn that 'inshallah' into 'alhamdulillah'. For the right-wing ops, that just means 'praise be to God.'"Republicans unable to win by distancing from TrumpThe defeat of Susan Collins, who has served as the Republican senator for Maine for three decades, was one indicator of the scale of the Republican losses. She was felled by Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, a logger who sought to point to his background to persuade blue-collar Mainers to vote for him.In a statement reported by US media, Collins conceded defeat and said it had been the "honour of my life" to serve the state for 30 years. The BBC's Helena Humphrey described a sombre atmosphere at Collins's watch party in the city of Maine - where the song Closing Time was played.Image source, ReutersImage caption, There was a sombre atmosphere at the watch party for Republican Susan CollinsCollins entered the race as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election, and found that her tactic to distance herself from Trump did not work.Ashley Hinson suffered the same fate in Iowa, losing that closely-fought Senate seat to Josh Turek. Hinson had slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important.History made by new black governors, first openly gay male senator and first Gen Z congresswomanAmong the other firsts of the night were in Florida, where Republican Byron Donalds has become the state's first black governor, following a hearty endorsement from Trump. Donalds, who will take over the job from Ron DeSantis, said his state was the "envy of the nation", and that he would work to make the state more affordable.The result was one of the few high points of an otherwise difficult evening for the Republicans. Image source, ReutersImage caption, A win for Bryon Donalds in Florida was one of the few high points for RepublicansIn the neighbouring state of Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, won the governor's race, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue. Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive. The state has also not had a Democratic governor for more than 20 years.Elsewhere, Democrat Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.Pappas defeated former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race, whom he thanked on Tuesday, saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."Figure caption, Watch: "I am ready to fight" - Senator-elect Chris Pappas celebrates New Hampshire winIn Colorado, Melat Kiros became the first woman elected to Congress from Gen Z - meaning those who were born between 1997 and 2012.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter.
